title: Solving quadratics by square roots
keyIdea: When a quadratic has only a squared term, or is written as a square equal to a number, you can solve it by square roots. First isolate the square, then take the square root of both sides and keep both signs: x² = k gives x = ±√k, and (x − p)² = q gives x = p ± √q. A positive k gives two real solutions, k = 0 gives one, and a negative k gives no real solutions.

kid: Solve x² = 25. You want a number that gives 25 when you square it. 5 works. But −5 works too, because −5 × −5 = 25. So x = 5 or x = −5. We write this as x = ±5.
On a graph, x² = 25 asks where the curve y = x² meets the line y = 25. The line cuts the curve twice, once on each side of the y-axis. Those two crossing points are the two solutions.

Move the line down and watch. At y = 0 it just touches the curve, so x² = 0 has one solution, x = 0. Below zero it misses the curve. No real number squared is negative, so x² = −4 has no real solutions.

Some equations need a tidy-up first. For 3x² − 12 = 36, add 12 to both sides to get 3x² = 48. Divide by 3 to get x² = 16. Only now take the square root: x = ±4. Get the square on its own first, then root it. A bracket works the same way. (x − 2)² = 25 means x − 2 is 5 or −5. So x = 7 or x = −3. In short, (x − p)² = q gives x = p ± √q. If q is not a square number, keep the root exact, like x = 1 ± √5.
adult: This topic sits in GCSE Mathematics (DfE 2013 subject content, A18: solve quadratic equations algebraically) and in Common Core A-REI.4.b, which asks students to solve quadratic equations by inspection, taking square roots and completing the square. It comes before factorising and the quadratic formula. It builds directly on solving x² = p from Key Stage 3.

Key terms: a quadratic equation has a squared term as its highest power. A solution, or root, is a value of x that makes the equation true. To isolate the square means to get x² or (x − p)² alone on one side. The ± sign records both square roots. The form (x − p)² = q is the completed-square form. Real solutions are where the graph crosses the line.

Common mistakes: writing only the positive root, so x² = 49 gives x = 7 and loses x = −7. Rooting before isolating, as if √(x² − 5) were x − √5. Halving instead of rooting, so x² = 50 becomes x = 25. Getting the sign of p wrong, so (x − 3)² = 16 gives x = −7 or 1. Claiming x² = −9 has solutions ±3, even though (−3)² = +9.

The lab links the algebra to the graph. Students drag the line y = k across y = x² and see ±√k appear. They find the cases k > 0, k = 0 and k < 0. They undo 3x² − 12 = 36 one step at a time, and early or one-sign roots are refused with reasons. Then they slide the parabola to solve (x − p)² = q and work backwards from two given solutions.

practice.hint: Which numbers give 64 when squared? Think about negative numbers too.
practice.explain: 8 × 8 = 64 and (−8) × (−8) = 64, so x = ±8. Squaring is undone by a square root, not by halving.

practice.prompt: Solve {a}x² = {=a*9}. What is the positive solution?
practice.hint: Divide both sides by {a} first so that x² is on its own, then take the square root.
practice.explain: Divide by {a}: x² = 9. Then x = ±3, so the positive solution is 3.

practice.prompt: What is a good first step to solve 2x² + 7 = 57?
choices: Take the square root of both sides
practice.hint: Get the squared term on its own before you take any square root.
practice.explain: Subtract 7: 2x² = 50. Divide by 2: x² = 25. Then x = ±5. Rooting first would wrongly split the root over +.

practice.prompt: Solve (x − {p})² = 25. What is the larger solution?
practice.hint: x − {p} must be 5 or −5. Add {p} to each.
practice.explain: x − {p} = ±5, so x = {p} + 5 = {=p+5} or x = {p} − 5 = {=p-5}. The larger solution is {=p+5}.

pool.hint: A positive number has two square roots.

pool.prompt: How many real solutions does x² = −16 have?
pool.hint: Can a real number squared ever be negative?
pool.explain: Any real number squared is 0 or more. (−4)² = +16, so x² = −16 has no real solutions.

pool.hint: Undo the − 11 before taking any root.
pool.explain: Add 11 to both sides: x² = 36. Then x = ±6.

pool.prompt: Solve x² = {=n*n}. What is the negative solution?
pool.hint: Find the positive square root of {=n*n} first, then use the minus sign.
pool.explain: {n}² = {=n*n}, so x = ±{n}. The negative solution is −{n}.

pool.prompt: Solve (x − {p})² = 16. What is the smaller solution?
pool.hint: x − {p} must be 4 or −4. Add {p} to each.
pool.explain: x − {p} = ±4, so x = {=p+4} or x = {=p-4}. The smaller solution is {=p-4}.

pool.hint: 5 is not a square number, so keep the square root as √5.
pool.explain: x − 1 = ±√5, so x = 1 + √5 or x = 1 − √5. These are exact; about 3.24 and −1.24.

pool.prompt: Which equation has exactly one real solution?
pool.hint: A square is zero only when the inside is zero.
pool.explain: (x − 5)² = 0 only when x − 5 = 0, so x = 5 is the one solution. x² = 5 has two; x² = −5 has none.

pool.prompt: Sam solves 4x² = 100 and writes x = ±10. What went wrong?
pool.hint: Get x² on its own first. Check: 4 × 10² = 400.
pool.explain: Divide by 4 first: x² = 25, so x = ±5. Check: 4 × 5² = 100. ±10 is the root of 100, not of 25.
